claims.text: A stable, homogeneous microstructure with high entropy of mixing enables lightweight high-entropy alloys to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
High entropy of mixing inhibits grain growth.
A stable, homogeneous, high-entropy microstructure promotes formation of a protective oxide layer.
The initial alloy is a single-phase solid solution containing elements such as Al, Cr, Fe, and Ni.
Controlled variation of alloying elements and processing conditions can optimize the alloy's microstructure and properties.
The proposed comparison should include high-temperature testing at approximately 800°C in air or an inert atmosphere.
The high-entropy alloy is predicted to have greater mechanical strength than the baseline alloy.
The high-entropy alloy is predicted to have greater corrosion resistance than the baseline alloy.
The high-entropy alloy is predicted to have greater high-temperature oxidation resistance than the baseline alloy.
The proposed baseline is a conventional binary or ternary alloy with similar composition but without the high-entropy effect.
Ineffective elemental mixing or improper processing leads to a non-homogeneous microstructure.
The proposed property-enhancement mechanism should cease to hold when the microstructure is non-homogeneous because of ineffective mixing or improper processing.
The exact relationship among alloying elements, microstructure, and properties is not fully understood.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing a high-entropy alloy and a baseline alloy under identical conditions.
Failure of the high-entropy alloy to improve the measured properties relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
